[PATH:empirical] A controlled experiment comparing coding output (e.g., lines of code, bug rates, task completion time) between remote and office settings, with clear goals and asynchronous tools, using professional developers as subjects. — Directly tests the hypothesis under the specified caveat, providing causal evidence for productivity differences.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on individual-focused task productivity in remote vs. office contexts, focusing on moderators like goal clarity and asynchronous tool use. — Synthesizes existing evidence across multiple studies to assess the generalizability and robustness of the hypothesized effect, identifying gaps or confounds.

qualifier.caveat: when clear goals and asynchronous collaboration tools are used

C004.subject: remote work under poor management practices
C004.object: office work under standard management practices
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work under poor management practices office work under standard management practices]

[PATH:empirical] Bloom, N., Liang, J., Roberts, J., & Ying, Z. J. (2015). 'Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment.' Quarterly Journal of Economics. — This landmark field experiment compared remote and office productivity under standard management, providing a baseline to evaluate how poor management (e.g., lack of oversight, feedback) degrades remote productivity relative to office norms.

[PATH:empirical] Choudhury, P., Foroughi, C., & Larson, B. (2021). 'Work-from-Anywhere: The Productivity Effects of Geographic Flexibility.' Strategic Management Journal. — This study examines productivity under different management conditions, offering data to test whether the negative effect of poor remote management (e.g., absent coordination) outweighs the productivity gains from flexibility seen under competent management.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of remote work productivity (e.g., Gajendran, R. S., & Harrison, D. A. (2007). 'The Good, the Bad, and the Unknown About Telecommuting.' Journal of Applied Psychology). — A systematic review can disaggregate effect sizes by management quality, testing whether poor remote management (e.g., lack of goal clarity, trust) systematically reduces productivity below office benchmarks.

qualifier.caveat: when managers lack experience in distributed team leadership

C005.subject: remote work for complex team coordination tasks
C005.object: office work for complex team coordination tasks
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work for complex team coordination tasks office work for complex team coordination tasks]

[PATH:empirical] Compare productivity outcomes of distributed agile teams with and without dedicated high-bandwidth video conferencing systems (e.g., always-on video, spatial audio) in controlled field experiments. — Directly tests the caveat (lack of synchronous infrastructure) as the moderating variable, measuring coordination quality and task completion time.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on remote vs. in-person collaboration for complex problem-solving tasks (e.g., design sprints, software architecture meetings), focusing on communication medium richness (e.g., Olson & Olson, 2000; recent turnover studies). — Synthesizes existing evidence to evaluate whether the productivity gap persists across communication quality levels, clarifying the disputed claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation modeling of team coordination under varying communication latency, bandwidth, and social presence parameters to predict productivity thresholds. — Provides a formal framework to identify boundary conditions where remote work might equal or underperform office work, especially when synchronous infrastructure is degraded.

C008.subject: remote work for complex team coordination tasks
C008.predicate: can achieve productivity comparable to or exceeding office work
C008.object: when implemented with high-quality coordination practices and tailored to team context
evidence_refs: [SYNTHESIS] Branch A highlights that remote work can outperform office work under certain conditions, while Branch B emphasizes parity. Both converge on the idea that remote work is at least as productive as office work, with variation depending on factors like team autonomy, communication tools, and task interdependence. Thus, the claim reframes the apparent contradiction by specifying the contextual moderators that determine whether remote work yields superiority or equivalence.
